n: Walking through grainfields on the Sabbath, Jesus’s hungry disciples pick heads of grain and eat. The law allowed this for travelers; the question was doing it on the Sabbath.

f.g: corn = grain, such as wheat or barley (not American maize).
an hungred = hungry.

n: The Pharisees count picking grain as harvesting — one of the kinds of work their traditions forbade on the Sabbath.

f.w: not lawful to do upon the sabbath day

n: Jesus answers from scripture, pointing to an episode in David’s life when he and his men were hungry.
David ate the holy bread from the sanctuary, normally reserved for priests. Human need was placed above ritual rule.

f.g: Twelve loaves set before the Lord in the sanctuary each Sabbath, later eaten by priests.

n: Priests work hard on the Sabbath — offering sacrifices — yet aren’t guilty, because their work serves God.

f.g: Technically break its rest by working.

n: A bold claim: something — someone — greater than the temple is present. If temple service justifies Sabbath work, how much more service to Jesus.
Jesus again quotes Hosea. Had the Pharisees understood that God prefers mercy, they wouldn’t have condemned innocent disciples.

f.w: I will have mercy, and not sacrifice

n: Jesus, as the Lord who gave the Sabbath, has authority to explain its true purpose.

f.w: Lord even of the sabbath day

n: Jesus enters a synagogue on the Sabbath — the setting for a second Sabbath controversy.

f.g: A local Jewish meeting place for prayer and scripture reading.

n: A man with a shriveled hand is there. Jesus’s critics use him as a test case, hoping to catch Jesus breaking their rules.

f.g: Shrunken and paralyzed.

n: Jesus points out their own practice: any of them would rescue a trapped sheep on the Sabbath.

f.w: lay hold on it, and lift it out

n: A person is worth far more than a sheep. So doing good — including healing — is right on the Sabbath.

f.w: it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days

n: Jesus simply tells the man to stretch out his hand, and as he obeys it is fully restored. Healing by a word involved no “work” at all.
Instead of rejoicing, the Pharisees begin plotting to kill Jesus — a sobering turning point.
Knowing their plot, Jesus withdraws, but crowds follow and he heals them all. Opposition doesn’t stop his compassion.
He asks those healed not to publicize him. He isn’t seeking fame or confrontation.
Matthew again explains Jesus’s quiet approach as fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy of the Lord’s servant.

f.g: Esaias = Isaiah.

n: Quoting Isaiah 42: God’s chosen, beloved servant, filled with the Spirit, will bring justice even to the Gentiles. The words echo the Father’s voice at Jesus’s baptism.

f.g: Here: justice, right order.

n: The servant won’t be loud or quarrelsome, drawing attention to himself in the streets.

f.g: strive = quarrel, wrangle.

n: He is infinitely gentle: he won’t snap a bent reed or snuff out a flickering wick. He tenderly preserves those who are weak and nearly spent.

f.g: A lamp wick that is barely burning.

n: Even Gentile nations will put their hope in his name — a hint of the worldwide mission to come.

f.w: in his name shall the Gentiles trust

n: Jesus heals a man made blind and mute by an evil spirit, so that he both sees and speaks.

f.g: dumb = unable to speak.

n: The amazed crowd begins asking whether Jesus could be the Messiah, the promised son of David.

f.w: Is not this the son of David?

n: Unable to deny the miracle, the Pharisees claim Jesus works by Satan’s power.

f.w: Beelzebub the prince of the devils

n: Jesus exposes the flaw in their logic: any kingdom, city, or family fighting itself will collapse.
Why would Satan defeat his own servants? That would destroy his own kingdom.
Other Jewish exorcists also cast out spirits. If the Pharisees’ logic were applied to them, they’d be condemned too.

f.g: Your followers or people of your own group.

n: If Jesus casts out devils by God’s Spirit, then God’s kingdom has arrived in their midst.

f.g: Luke has “the finger of God,” recalling Exodus 8:19.

n: To rob a strong man, you must first tie him up. Jesus is overpowering Satan and freeing those Satan held captive.

f.g: spoil = plunder, carry off.

n: There is no neutral ground with Christ. Those who don’t help him gather people are, in effect, scattering them.

f.w: He that is not with me is against me

n: God forgives every kind of sin and even blasphemy if people repent — except blasphemy against the Holy Ghost.

f.w: the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost

n: Speaking against Jesus in ignorance can be forgiven. Latter-day Saint teaching explains the unpardonable sin as knowingly denying Christ after receiving a sure witness from the Holy Ghost.

f.w: neither in this world, neither in the world to come

n: Jesus returns to his tree image: be consistent. Good trees bear good fruit. His good works show where his power comes from.

f.w: the tree is known by his fruit

n: Words reveal the heart. The Pharisees’ slander came from what filled their hearts.

f.g: Offspring of snakes — the same rebuke John the Baptist used.

f.w: out of the abundance of the heart

n: Each heart is a storehouse. What we fill it with determines what we bring out.

f.g: A storeroom or treasury.

n: We are accountable for our words, even careless ones. Words matter because they flow from who we are.

f.g: A careless, useless, or harmful word.

n: Our words will be evidence in judgment — either declaring us righteous or condemning us.

f.g: justified = declared right, acquitted.

n: Right after this miracle, some scribes and Pharisees demand a sign — proof on their terms.
Jesus calls sign-seeking a mark of spiritual unfaithfulness. The only sign they’ll get is that of Jonah.

f.g: Unfaithful to God, as a spouse breaks a marriage covenant.
Jonas = Jonah.

n: Jonah’s three days inside the great fish foreshadow Jesus’s three days in the tomb before rising.

f.g: A Jewish way of reckoning that counted any part of a day as a day.
Greek kētos — a great sea creature.

n: Pagan Nineveh repented when Jonah preached. Jesus, far greater, preaches to Israel, which refuses to repent.
The queen of Sheba traveled far to hear Solomon’s wisdom. One far wiser than Solomon is here, and they won’t listen.

f.g: The queen of Sheba, probably from southern Arabia.

n: Jesus describes an evil spirit cast out of a person, wandering in desolate places and finding no rest.

f.g: Deserts, thought to be haunts of evil spirits.

n: Returning, the spirit finds its old “house” clean and tidy — but empty. Nothing good has moved in.

f.g: garnished = decorated, put in order.

n: It brings seven worse spirits, and the person ends up worse than before. Removing evil isn’t enough; we must fill our lives with God. Jesus applies this to his generation.

f.w: the last state of that man is worse than the first

n: Mary and Jesus’s brothers arrive and wait outside, wanting to speak with him.

f.g: Jesus’s younger half-brothers, sons of Mary and Joseph.
without = outside.

n: Someone passes the message along to Jesus.
Jesus uses the moment to teach — not rejecting his family, but redefining what family means in God’s kingdom.
Pointing to his disciples, he says these are his family too.

f.w: Behold my mother and my brethren!

n: Anyone who does the Father’s will becomes part of Jesus’s family — a bond as close as mother, brother, or sister.

f.w: whosoever shall do the will of my Father
